lessons.title: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers

blocks.md:
Machine learning is full of uncertainty: a label may be noisy, a click may or may not happen, a language model outputs a *distribution* over the next **token** (a word or piece of a word). Probability is the bookkeeping for that uncertainty, and statistics is how you learn its numbers from data. This course builds both from scratch, with one small running example per lesson.

It starts where every analysis starts: you already have a pile of numbers and need to say what they look like.

Ten requests to a service took these times, sorted, in milliseconds: 38, 41, 42, 44, 45, 47, 49, 52, 55, 58.

- The **mean** (average) is the sum divided by the count: $471 / 10 = 47.1$ ms.
- The **median** is the middle value of the sorted data. With an even count it is the average of the two middle values, here $(45 + 47)/2 = 46$ ms.

Now suppose the last request hit a slow disk and took 900 ms instead of 58.

blocks.prompt: Replace 58 ms with 900 ms. Roughly how far do the mean and the median move?
blocks.reveal: **The mean jumps from 47.1 to 131.3 ms; the median stays at 46 ms.** One value out of ten dragged the mean above 9 of the 10 requests, so the mean no longer describes a typical request. The median depends only on the order of the values, not on how far out the extreme one lies, so it does not care whether the slow request took 58 ms or 58 seconds.

blocks.title: Mean, median and p90 of ten latencies, before and after one outlier

scenes.caption: Ten well-behaved requests: mean 47.1 ms, median 46 ms, 90th percentile 55.3 ms. All three tell a similar story.
One request becomes 900 ms. The mean jumps to 131.3 ms and the p90 to 139.5 ms, while the median does not move at all.

blocks.md:
A **percentile** is a value with a given share of the data below it: about 90% of values lie below the 90th percentile, written **p90**. The word comes from *per cent*, "per hundred": percentiles split sorted data into hundredths. The median is p50; p90, p99 and p99.9 describe the slow tail that latency dashboards watch. A **quantile** is the same idea with a fraction instead of a percentage: the 0.9 quantile is p90.

With ten points, the 90th percentile usually falls *between* two data points, so a rule has to interpolate, and the handbook of NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) notes there is no single universally accepted rule.

blocks.tex: h = (n-1)\,q, \qquad Q(q) = x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor)} + \big(h - \lfloor h \rfloor\big)\big(x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor + 1)} - x_{(\lfloor h \rfloor)}\big)
blocks.caption: NumPy's default "linear" rule, with x(0) to x(n-1) the sorted data counted from 0. In words: find the fractional position h, then go that fraction of the way to the next sorted value. For p90 of 10 points, h = 9 x 0.9 = 8.1.

blocks.title: Percentiles are positions in the sorted data

scenes.caption: Sorted latencies, positions 0 to 9. The median sits halfway between positions 4 and 5: (45 + 47) / 2 = 46 ms.
p90 by the linear rule: position h = 8.1, so take 55 and go 10% of the way to 58: 55 + 0.1 x 3 = 55.3 ms.
Make the last value 900. Now 10% of the way from 55 to 900 is 139.5 ms. NIST's default rule counts positions from 1, so p90 sits at 0.9 x 11 = 9.9: 90% of the way from 55 to 900, or 815.5 ms.

blocks.md: The two rules disagree wildly here, 139.5 vs 815.5 ms, because with ten points the 90th percentile is decided by the top two values and the interpolation rule. NumPy offers many methods through `np.percentile(x, q, method=...)`; its default is `"linear"`, and `"weibull"` matches the NIST handbook's default. For a reliable p99 you need many hundreds of samples, since only 1 in 100 lies beyond it.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

lat = np.array([38, 41, 42, 44, 45, 47, 49, 52, 55, 900])  # ms, sorted
print("mean  ", lat.mean())
print("median", np.median(lat))
print("p90   ", round(np.percentile(lat, 90), 1))                     # method="linear"
print("p90 w ", round(np.percentile(lat, 90, method="weibull"), 1))   # NIST's p(N+1) rule
q1, q3 = np.percentile(lat, [25, 75])
print("IQR   ", q3 - q1)
print("std   ", round(lat.std(ddof=1), 1))
blocks.caption: Output: mean 131.3, median 46.0, p90 139.5, p90 w 815.5, IQR 8.75, std 270.1. The outlier dominates the mean and the standard deviation but leaves the median and the IQR untouched.

blocks.md: Spread needs a summary too. The **range** is max minus min: 20 ms before the outlier, 862 ms after. The **interquartile range** (IQR) is p75 minus p25, the width of the middle half of the data (a *quartile* cuts the data into quarters): 8.75 ms both before and after. The **standard deviation**, roughly the typical distance from the mean (lesson 5 defines it exactly), goes from 6.4 to 270 ms. Statistics built on ranks, such as the median and IQR, are called **robust** because a few extreme values barely move them.

blocks.title: 1,000 simulated latencies: histogram, then cumulative share

scenes.caption: A **histogram** counts values per bin, shown here as a share of all 1,000 latencies. They were simulated from a skewed model with median near 50 ms: most land in 25 to 75 ms, with a long tail to the right.
Same data as an **empirical CDF**: the share of values at or below each bin's upper edge. It climbs to 0.935 by 100 ms. p90 (88 ms) is where it crosses 0.9; p99 (143 ms) is where it crosses 0.99.

blocks.md: Data like this, with a long right tail, is called **right-skewed**. The NIST handbook notes that in a skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the heavier tail: here the mean is 53.9 ms while the median is 48.3 ms. Latencies, incomes and file sizes all look like this. That is why a latency report shows p50 for the typical request and p99 for the unlucky ones, instead of one mean that describes neither.

Percentiles do not average. The p99 of two servers combined is not the mean of their two p99 values: it depends on how many requests each served and on the shape of both tails. Compute percentiles from the merged raw data (or from merged histograms).
The mean answers "total divided by count", the median answers "what is typical", and tail percentiles answer "how bad is it for the unlucky few". For skewed data, report more than the mean.

blocks.question: A service reports a median latency of 40 ms and a mean of 95 ms. What does this most likely indicate?
options: About half the requests take close to 95 ms
The median must be wrong, since the mean and the median have to agree
Most requests take longer than 95 ms
A small share of very slow requests pulls the mean far above the typical request
blocks.explain: Half the requests take 40 ms or less, so a mean of 95 ms needs some very large values: the data are right-skewed. The mean and the median agree only for symmetric data, such as a normal distribution.

blocks.question: You have 20 latency samples and want to put p99 on a dashboard. What is the main problem?
options: p99 of 20 values is decided by the largest one or two values and the interpolation rule, so it is mostly noise
p99 cannot be computed for fewer than 100 values
p99 always equals the maximum, so it adds no information
Nothing, as long as you use NumPy's default method
blocks.explain: Any rule returns a number, but with 20 samples p99 is an interpolation between the top two values, and different methods give very different answers. Only 1 in 100 values lies beyond p99, so you need many hundreds of samples before it is stable.

lessons.title: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does

blocks.md: The previous lesson summarized numbers you already had. Probability runs the other way: it starts from a model of chance and says how likely each outcome is.

Start with the simplest model of chance: roll two fair six-sided dice. The **sample space** is the set of all possible outcomes, here the 36 ordered pairs (first die, second die). An **event** is a subset of outcomes, such as "the sum is 7". When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just counting:

- $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{outcomes in } A}{\text{total outcomes}}$

Every probability lies between 0 and 1, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of non-overlapping events add.

blocks.title: Two dice: 36 equally likely outcomes, colored by their sum

scenes.caption: Each cell is one outcome; the number is the sum of the two dice. All 36 cells are equally likely, each with probability 1/36.
Event A: sum is 7. Six cells lie on the anti-diagonal, so P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6, about 0.167. No other sum has as many cells.
Event B: sum is at least 10. Also six cells (10, 11, 12), so P(B) = 6/36 = 1/6 as well.
Now condition on C: the first die shows 6. The other 30 outcomes are ruled out, so the new sample space is one row of 6 cells. Three of them have sum at least 10, so P(B | C) = 3/6 = 0.5.
Same row, event A instead. Only one of the 6 cells sums to 7, so P(A | C) = 1/6, exactly the unconditional P(A). Learning C changed B's probability but not A's.

blocks.md: **Conditional probability** $P(A \mid C)$ is the probability of $A$ once you know $C$ happened. Knowing $C$ shrinks the sample space to $C$, so you count $A$ only inside it. $A \cap C$ is the event that both $A$ and $C$ happen: the outcomes that lie in both sets (the cap symbol is read "intersect"). Its probability $P(A \cap C)$ is called the **joint probability** of $A$ and $C$. The general rule, which works even when outcomes are not equally likely, is the ratio below.

blocks.tex: P(A \mid C) = \frac{P(A \cap C)}{P(C)}, \qquad P(A \cap C) = P(A \mid C)\,P(C)
blocks.caption: Definition of conditional probability (for P(C) greater than 0) and the multiplication rule it implies: inside C, the share of C that is also A.

blocks.md: Check it on the figure: $P(B \cap C) = 3/36$ and $P(C) = 6/36$, so $P(B \mid C) = 3/6$. Two events are **independent** when knowing one does not change the other: $P(A \mid C) = P(A)$, which is the same as $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$. The two dice themselves are independent, which is why each cell has probability $\frac16 \times \frac16 = \frac1{36}$.

blocks.prompt: Is "sum is 7" independent of "first die is 6"? Is "sum is at least 10" independent of it?
blocks.reveal:
**Sum is 7: yes, independent.** $P(A \cap C) = 1/36 = (1/6)(1/6) = P(A)P(C)$. Whatever the first die shows, exactly one value of the second die makes 7.

**Sum at least 10: no.** $P(B \cap C) = 3/36 = 0.083$, but $P(B)P(C) = 1/36 = 0.028$. A high first die makes a high sum more likely. Independence is a numeric fact about probabilities, not an intuition about whether events "feel related".

blocks.md: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Mutually exclusive events ("sum is 2" and "sum is 12") cannot both happen, so learning one happened tells you the other did not: they are strongly *dependent*. Independence means the joint probability factorizes, $P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C)$.
Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

blocks.question: A model's training set has 1,000 emails: 300 are spam, and 240 of the spam emails contain the word "free". Of the 700 non-spam emails, 70 contain "free". What is P(spam | contains "free")?
options: 0.80, because 240 of 300 spam emails contain free
0.24, because 240 of 1,000 emails are spam with free
About 0.77, because 240 of the 310 emails containing free are spam
0.30, the base rate of spam
blocks.explain: Condition on the event you observed: restrict to the 240 + 70 = 310 emails containing "free", of which 240 are spam, so 240/310 = 0.774. Option A is P(free | spam), the reverse conditional, a very common mix-up that the next lesson is about.

blocks.question: You flip a fair coin twice. Let A = "first flip is heads" and B = "the two flips match". Are A and B independent?
options: No, because B depends on the first flip
Yes: P(A and B) = 1/4 = P(A) P(B)
No, because A and B can both happen
It cannot be determined without more data
blocks.explain: P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 2/4 = 1/2 (HH or TT), and P(A and B) = P(HH) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B). Even though B is defined using the first flip, it is independent of A. Independence is checked with numbers, not by whether one event is mentioned in the other's definition.

lessons.title: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong

blocks.md: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test catches 90% of sick people (its **sensitivity**, $P(+ \mid \text{sick})$) and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people (its **false positive rate**, $P(+ \mid \text{healthy})$). Your test comes back positive. How likely is it that you are sick?

blocks.prompt: Guess before reading on: is P(sick | positive) closer to 90%, 50%, or 10%?
blocks.reveal: **About 9%.** Most people guess near 90% because they read the sensitivity $P(+ \mid \text{sick})$ as if it were $P(\text{sick} \mid +)$. Those are different conditionals, and the gap between them is set by the **base rate**: how common the disease is to begin with.

blocks.title: 10,000 people through the test (counts, not percentages)

scenes.caption: Picture 10,000 people. The base rate splits them first: 1% sick gives 100 sick and 9,900 healthy.
Of the 100 sick, the test catches 90% (90 true positives) and misses 10.
Of the 9,900 healthy, 9% still test positive: 891 false positives. A small rate applied to a huge group gives a big count.
A positive result puts you among 90 + 891 = 981 positives, only 90 of whom are sick: 90 / 981 = 9.2%. The false positives outnumber the true ones about 10 to 1.

blocks.md: **Bayes' rule**, named after Thomas Bayes, whose essay on it was published in 1763, is the same calculation in symbols. It flips a conditional you know, $P(E \mid H)$ (evidence given hypothesis), into the one you want, $P(H \mid E)$. It follows in one line from the multiplication rule of the previous lesson: $P(H \cap E)$ can be written both as $P(H \mid E)P(E)$ and as $P(E \mid H)P(H)$, so dividing the second by $P(E)$ gives $P(H \mid E)$. The denominator $P(E)$ sums over every way the evidence can arise: here, sick and positive plus healthy and positive.

blocks.caption: In words: P(sick given positive) is the sick-and-positive probability, 0.9 times 0.01 = 0.009, divided by the total chance of a positive, 0.009 + 0.09 times 0.99 = 0.0981. That is about 0.092, the same as 90 of 981 people. Prior P(sick) = 0.01, likelihoods 0.9 and 0.09, posterior about 0.092.

blocks.md: The vocabulary carries over to all of ML. The **prior** $P(H)$ is what you believed before the evidence. The **likelihood** $P(E \mid H)$ says how well each hypothesis predicts the evidence. The **posterior** $P(H \mid E)$ is the updated belief. Drag the prior below and watch how strongly the answer depends on it.

blocks.title: Posterior after one positive test, as the base rate changes

scenes.caption: With sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09, the same positive test means 1.0% at a 0.1% base rate, 9.2% at 1%, 52.6% at 10% and 90.9% at 50%.
Cut the false positive rate to 0.01 and the 1% case jumps to about 48%. For rare conditions, false positives matter far more than sensitivity.
Back at 0.09 but sensitivity raised to 0.99: the 1% case only moves to about 10%. Catching more sick people barely helps when the healthy group is 99 times larger.

blocks.md: Evidence also stacks. After the first positive, your belief is 9.2%; use that as the prior for a second test. If tests are **conditionally independent** given disease status (an assumption: repeating the same flawed test usually is not), each positive multiplies the **odds** of being sick, $P(\text{sick}) / P(\text{healthy})$, by the **likelihood ratio** $0.9 / 0.09 = 10$. Why: write Bayes' rule once for sick and once for healthy and divide the two; the shared denominator $P(+)$ cancels, leaving posterior odds equal likelihood ratio times prior odds. Here 1 to 99 becomes 10 to 99, and 10 / 109 is the 9.2%.

blocks.title: Belief in sick after repeated positive tests

scenes.caption: Before testing, the belief is the base rate: 1%.
One positive: 9.2%. Still more likely healthy than sick.
A second, independent positive: 50.3%. The posterior from step one became the prior for step two.
A third: 91.0%. Each test multiplied the odds by 10, from 1:99 to about 10:1.

blocks.md: The classic mistake is confusing $P(E \mid H)$ with $P(H \mid E)$, called base rate neglect. It shows up in ML with a classifier on a rare class. Its **recall** is $P(\text{flagged} \mid \text{positive class})$, the sensitivity, and does not depend on the base rate; its **precision** is $P(\text{positive class} \mid \text{flagged})$, the posterior, and does. High recall can still come with mostly false alarms.
Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

blocks.question: A fraud model flags 95% of fraudulent transactions and 2% of legitimate ones. Fraud is 0.1% of transactions. Roughly what fraction of flagged transactions are fraud?
options: About 95%
About 50%
About 4.5%
About 0.1%
blocks.explain: Per 100,000 transactions: 100 fraud, 95 flagged; 99,900 legitimate, 1,998 flagged. 95 / (95 + 1,998) = 0.045. The flagging rate on fraud (95%) is recall, not precision; the tiny base rate makes most flags false alarms.

blocks.question: Which change most increases P(sick | positive) for a disease with a 1% base rate, starting from sensitivity 0.9 and false positive rate 0.09?
options: Raise sensitivity to 0.99
Lower the false positive rate to 0.01
Both help equally
Neither, the base rate fixes the answer
blocks.explain: Raising sensitivity takes the posterior from 9.2% to about 10%. Lowering the false positive rate to 0.01 takes it to about 48%, because false positives come from the 99% healthy group and dominate the positives.

lessons.title: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability

blocks.md: Go back to the 1,000 emails from the quiz in lesson 2: 300 spam, 240 of them containing "free", and 70 of the 700 non-spam emails containing "free". Two yes/no facts describe each email. Their **joint distribution** gives the probability of every combination, such as $P(\text{spam}, \text{free}) = 240/1000 = 0.24$. The four cells sum to 1.

blocks.title: Spam by the word "free": joint table with its margins

scenes.caption: The joint table: each cell is the probability of one combination. 0.24 + 0.06 + 0.07 + 0.63 = 1.
Sum the spam row: P(spam) = 0.24 + 0.06 = 0.30, written in the right margin. That is a marginal probability.
Sum the free column: P(free) = 0.24 + 0.07 = 0.31, written in the bottom margin.
Condition on free: keep only that column and divide by its total. P(spam | free) = 0.24 / 0.31 = 0.774, the quiz answer from lesson 2.

blocks.md: Summing a joint table over the variable you do not care about gives the **marginal distribution** of the one you do. The name is literal: with the table on paper, you write each row's and column's sum in the margin. A **conditional distribution** is one row or column divided by its total, the renormalizing from lesson 2.

blocks.tex: P(X = x) = \sum_{y} P(X = x,\, Y = y), \qquad P(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X = x)}
blocks.caption: The sum rule (marginalizing; the big Sigma means add the terms for every value y) and the definition of a conditional, written for random quantities X and Y instead of single events.

blocks.md: Write each joint cell with the multiplication rule, $P(E, H) = P(E \mid H)P(H)$, then sum a column, and you get the **law of total probability**: $P(E) = \sum_h P(E \mid H = h)\,P(H = h)$. That is exactly the denominator of Bayes' rule in lesson 3: $P(+) = 0.9 \times 0.01 + 0.09 \times 0.99 = 0.0981$, the sick-and-positive cell plus the healthy-and-positive cell. Bayes' rule is just a joint cell divided by its column total.

The multiplication rule also chains. Apply it twice and any joint probability splits into one-variable conditionals, each conditioned on everything before it. This **chain rule of probability** works for any number of variables and in any order. It is how a language model defines the probability of a whole text: the probability of each token given all earlier tokens, multiplied together.

blocks.tex: P(a, b, c) = P(a)\,P(b \mid a)\,P(c \mid a, b), \qquad P(w_1, \dots, w_n) = \prod_{k=1}^{n} P(w_k \mid w_1, \dots, w_{k-1})
blocks.caption: In words: the chance of the whole sequence is the chance of the first item, times the chance of the second given the first, and so on. The big Pi means multiply the terms, as a big Sigma means add them.

blocks.title: Scoring "the cat sat" with the chain rule (toy probabilities)

scenes.caption: A made-up model gives P(the) = 0.05 as a first token. Its natural log is -3.00.
P(cat | the) = 0.01. Multiplying probabilities is adding logs: running log-probability -3.00 + (-4.61) = -7.60.
P(sat | the cat) = 0.2. Total log-probability -9.21, which is ln of 0.05 x 0.01 x 0.2 = 0.0001.

blocks.md: Real texts have thousands of tokens, and a product of thousands of probabilities below 1 underflows to 0 in floating point. Adding logs instead avoids that, so models work with **log-probabilities**. Minus the average log-probability per token is the training loss you will meet in lesson 9.

Two variables are **conditionally independent** given a third, $Z$, if $P(x, y \mid z) = P(x \mid z)\,P(y \mid z)$ for every value $z$: once you know $Z$, learning $X$ tells you nothing more about $Y$. The **naive Bayes** classifier assumes the words of a document are conditionally independent given its class. It is called naive because real words are not; the assumption is what lets it multiply one probability per word.

Add a second word, "winner": it appears in 60 of the 300 spam emails and 7 of the 700 others.

blocks.caption: Naive Bayes for an email containing both "free" and "winner" (ham means not spam). In words: prior times one likelihood per word, for each class, then divide by the total so the two posteriors sum to 1.

blocks.prompt: Flip two fair coins: they are independent. Now someone tells you at least one landed heads. Are the two coins still independent?
blocks.reveal: **No.** Given "at least one heads", the possible outcomes are HH, HT, TH, equally likely. $P(\text{first is H}) = 2/3$. But if you also learn the second is tails, the first *must* be heads: probability 1. If the second is heads, the first is H with probability 1/2. Conditioning on a common effect made two independent causes dependent. The same thing happens in filtered data, such as only the items users clicked or only the papers accepted, where correlations can appear that do not exist in the full population.

blocks.md: Independence and conditional independence are different, and neither implies the other. The coins above are independent but become dependent once you condition. Two tests on the same patient (lesson 3) go the other way: dependent overall, since both tend to be positive for sick people, but possibly independent once disease status is known.
The joint table holds everything. Marginals are its row and column sums, conditionals are a row or column divided by its total, and the chain rule rebuilds the joint from one-variable conditionals.

blocks.question: Using the spam table (0.24, 0.06, 0.07, 0.63), what is P(contains free | not spam)?
options: 0.07, the joint cell
0.31, the share of all emails containing free
0.23, which is 70 of the 310 emails containing free
0.10, which is 70 of the 700 non-spam emails
blocks.explain: Condition on not spam: take that row (0.07 and 0.63, total 0.70) and divide: 0.07 / 0.70 = 0.10. Option C divides by the wrong total: it is P(not spam | free), the reversed conditional.

blocks.question: A language model gives probabilities 0.2, 0.5 and 0.1 to three successive tokens, each conditioned on the tokens before it. What is the total log-probability (natural log) of the three tokens?
options: About -4.61, the sum of the three logs, equal to ln 0.01
About -1.54, the average of the three logs
0.8, the sum of the three probabilities
About -2.30, the log of the smallest probability
blocks.explain: By the chain rule the joint probability is 0.2 x 0.5 x 0.1 = 0.01, and the log of a product is the sum of logs: -1.61 - 0.69 - 2.30 = -4.61. The average, -1.54 per token, is minus the cross-entropy per token used as a training loss.

lessons.title: Random variables, expected value and variance

blocks.md: A **random variable** is a number attached to each outcome: the value of a die, the number of clicks out of 8 impressions (times an item is shown to a user), a model's loss on a random training example. Its **distribution** lists the probability of each value. For a discrete variable this is the **probability mass function** (PMF), $P(X = k)$, and the values sum to 1.

Two numbers summarize a distribution. The **expected value** (mean) $E[X]$ is the probability-weighted average of its values: where the distribution balances. The **variance** $\text{Var}(X)$ is the expected squared distance from the mean: how spread out it is. The **standard deviation** $\sigma$ is the square root of the variance, in the same units as $X$.

blocks.caption: In words: the mean adds up each value times its probability. The variance is the mean of the squared distance from the mean; expanding the square shows it also equals the mean of X squared minus the square of the mean.

blocks.md:
One fair die: $E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5$, a value the die never shows, which is fine since it is an average. For the variance use the second form: $E[X^2] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 \approx 15.17$, minus $3.5^2 = 12.25$, gives $\text{Var}(X) = 35/12 \approx 2.92$ and $\sigma \approx 1.71$. (Why the two forms agree: expanding the square gives $E[(X-\mu)^2] = E[X^2] - 2\mu E[X] + \mu^2$, and since $E[X] = \mu$ that is $E[X^2] - \mu^2$.)

A **Bernoulli** variable is 1 with probability $p$ and 0 otherwise (a click, a correct prediction). It is named after the mathematician Jacob Bernoulli. Its mean is $1 \times p + 0 \times (1-p) = p$. Since $X^2 = X$ when $X$ is 0 or 1, $E[X^2] = p$ too, so its variance is $p - p^2 = p(1-p)$, largest at $p = 0.5$.

Add up $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) trials and you get a **binomial** variable: the number of successes, with $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$. Any one sequence with $k$ successes has probability $p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$, by multiplying independent trials. The **binomial coefficient** $\binom{n}{k}$ counts the ways to choose which $k$ of the $n$ trials succeed, which is how many such sequences there are; it equals $\frac{n!}{k!\,(n-k)!}$, where $n!$ (read n factorial) is $n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 1$.

blocks.title: Binomial PMF: number of clicks in n = 8 impressions

scenes.caption: Click probability p = 0.3. The most likely count is 2, and the mean is np = 2.4 with variance np(1 - p) = 1.68.
p = 0.5: symmetric around the mean of 4, variance 2.0. This is the widest of the three because p(1 - p) peaks at p = 0.5.
p = 0.8: mean 6.4, variance 1.28. The mass piles up against the maximum of 8, so the shape skews left.

blocks.md: Two rules make expectations easy to compute. **Linearity of expectation**: $E[aX + bY] = aE[X] + bE[Y]$ for any random variables, independent or not. That is why the binomial mean is just $n$ copies of $p$. **Variances add for independent variables**: $\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$ when $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and $\text{Var}(aX) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X)$. So the binomial variance is $n$ copies of $p(1-p)$: $np(1-p)$.

Linearity is most useful when the pieces are dependent. Shuffle $n$ cards numbered 1 to $n$: how many land in their own position (a **fixed point**)? Write the count as a sum of **indicator** variables, $I_k = 1$ if card $k$ lands in position $k$ and 0 otherwise. Each $I_k$ is Bernoulli with $p = 1/n$, so linearity gives $E[\text{count}] = n \times 1/n = 1$, for every $n$. The indicators are dependent (if cards 1 to $n-1$ are all in place, card $n$ must be too), yet the answer never needed that dependence.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, trials = 10, 100_000
fixed = [(rng.permutation(n) == np.arange(n)).sum() for _ in range(trials)]
print("mean fixed points:", np.mean(fixed))
print("P(no fixed point):", np.mean(np.array(fixed) == 0))
blocks.caption: Output: mean fixed points 1.0006, P(no fixed point) 0.36694. The simulated mean matches 1; the chance of no match at all is close to 1/e = 0.368, the classic answer to this matching problem.

blocks.prompt: You roll two dice and add them. What are the mean and variance of the sum? What if you instead roll one die and double it?
blocks.reveal:
Two dice: mean $3.5 + 3.5 = 7$, variance $35/12 + 35/12 \approx 5.83$.

One die doubled: the mean is still 7, but the variance is $2^2 \times 35/12 \approx 11.67$, twice as large. The two independent dice partly cancel each other's luck; doubling one die copies its luck. This is the seed of why averaging many independent samples reduces noise (lesson 7).

blocks.md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

Every variable so far took separate values you could list: 0, 1, 2 and so on. A latency of 47.3 ms is different, because between any two values there are infinitely many others. The next lesson handles those continuous variables.

blocks.question: A large language model (LLM) evaluation has 200 independent questions and the model answers each correctly with probability 0.7. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number correct?
options: Mean 140, standard deviation 42
Mean 140, standard deviation about 6.5
Mean 0.7, standard deviation 0.21
Mean 140, standard deviation 0.46
blocks.explain: Binomial with n = 200, p = 0.7: mean np = 140, variance np(1 - p) = 42, so the standard deviation is the square root, about 6.48. Option A forgets the square root. Runs of the same eval can differ by several questions from noise alone.

blocks.question: X is a die roll and Y = 7 - X (the face on the opposite side). What is Var(X + Y)?
options: Undefined, because X and Y are dependent
blocks.explain: X + Y = 7 always, a constant, so its variance is 0. Adding the variances (35/6) would be wrong because X and Y are perfectly negatively correlated, and the covariance term cancels them exactly. Linearity still gives E[X + Y] = 7.

lessons.title: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions

blocks.md: A latency can be 47.3 ms or 47.31 ms or anything in between. With infinitely many possible values, each exact value has probability 0, so $P(X = 47.3) = 0$, and the useful questions are about ranges: what is $P(45 \le X \le 50)$? Tiny example: a spinner stops at a uniformly random point in $[0, 1)$. The chance it stops between 0.2 and 0.5 is that interval's length, 0.3.

The **cumulative distribution function** (CDF) is $F(x) = P(X \le x)$: it accumulates probability from the left, hence *cumulative*. It works for every kind of variable, and every range probability is a subtraction of two CDF values. For the spinner, $F(x) = x$ on $[0, 1]$, so $P(0.2 < X \le 0.5) = 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3$. The empirical CDF of lesson 1 is the same idea computed from data.

blocks.tex: F(x) = P(X \le x), \qquad P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a), \qquad P(x < X \le x + h) \approx f(x)\,h \ \text{ for small } h
blocks.caption: The CDF, range probabilities as differences, and the density f(x): probability per unit length near x. If you know integrals, F(b) - F(a) is the integral of f from a to b, the area under the density.

blocks.md: The **probability density function** (PDF) $f(x)$ is probability per unit length, as mass density is mass per unit volume. It is the slope of the CDF. A density is not a probability, so it can exceed 1: a variable uniform on $[0, 0.5]$ has density 2 there, because the total area, width 0.5 times height 2, must be 1. Probabilities are areas under the density, which the CDF has already added up for you.

The **exponential** distribution models waiting times between independent random events, such as requests arriving at an average **rate** $\lambda$ per second. The chance of waiting longer than $t$ is $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, so $F(t) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$, the density is $\lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ and the mean wait is $1/\lambda$. At $\lambda = 2$ per second: mean wait 0.5 s, $P(T \le 0.5) = 1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$, $P(T > 1) = e^{-2} = 0.135$. The median, $\ln 2 / 2 = 0.35$ s, is below the mean: right-skewed, as in lesson 1.

blocks.title: Exponential waiting times: density and CDF

scenes.caption: Rate 2 per second. The density starts at 2, above 1, which is fine for a density. The CDF reads F(0.5) = 0.632 and F(1) = 0.865, so 13.5% of waits exceed 1 s.
Rate 1 per second: slower arrivals, a mean wait of 1 s. The density is flatter and the CDF climbs more slowly: F(1) = 0.632.
Rate 4 per second: the density starts at 4 and the CDF reaches 0.98 by 1 s. Whatever the rate, the area under the density is 1 and the CDF ends at 1.

blocks.prompt: Requests arrive at rate 2 per second with exponential waits. You have already waited 1 second with nothing. What is the chance you wait more than another 0.5 s?
blocks.reveal: **Still 0.368, as if you had just started.** $P(T > 1.5 \mid T > 1) = e^{-3} / e^{-2} = e^{-1} = 0.368 = P(T > 0.5)$. The exponential is **memoryless**: time already waited tells you nothing about the remaining wait. A scheduled train that comes every 12 minutes is not like that: after 5 minutes of waiting, it is closer.

blocks.md: The **normal** distribution, also called Gaussian after the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ is the bell curve. To get its probabilities, **standardize**: $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ counts standard deviations from the mean, and $Z$ then has the **standard normal** distribution (mean 0, standard deviation 1). Its CDF is written $\Phi$ (capital Greek phi). It has no simple formula, so you read it from a table or call `scipy.stats.norm.cdf`. Example: if eval scores are normal with mean 70 and standard deviation 10, then $P(X > 85) = 1 - \Phi(1.5) = 0.067$.

blocks.caption: Normal density. In words: the height falls off with the squared distance from mu, measured in units of sigma, so the curve is a symmetric bell; the factor in front makes the total area 1. About 68.3% of the mass is within 1 sigma of the mean, 95.4% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.

blocks.title: Reading tail areas from the standard normal

scenes.caption: Phi(1) = 0.841, so the area between -1 and 1 is 0.841 - 0.159 = 0.683: about 68% of a normal lies within 1 standard deviation.
Phi(1.96) = 0.975: 2.5% lies above 1.96 and, by symmetry, 2.5% below -1.96. That is where the 1.96 in every 95% interval of this course comes from.
z = 2.02: the two tails beyond plus or minus 2.02 hold 2 x (1 - Phi(2.02)) = 0.043. Lesson 12 calls this number a p-value.

blocks.md:
Discrete companions you will meet next to these:

- **Bernoulli** and **binomial** (lesson 5): one yes/no trial, and the count of successes in $n$ trials.
- **Categorical**: one of $k$ labels, with probabilities summing to 1. A language model's next-token output is a categorical distribution over its vocabulary.
- **Poisson**($\lambda$), after the mathematician Simeon Denis Poisson: the number of events in a fixed interval, when events happen independently at an average of $\lambda$ per interval. Mean $\lambda$, standard deviation $\sqrt{\lambda}$, and $P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k / k!$. If arrivals are Poisson, the gaps between them are exponential.

blocks.title: Poisson(3): requests per second at an average of 3

scenes.caption: P(k) = e^-3 3^k / k!. Exactly 2 and exactly 3 requests are equally likely (0.224 each); a quiet second with 0 requests has probability 0.050.
P(6 or more) = 0.084: in about 1 second out of 12, traffic is at least twice the average, from chance alone (the bars shown, 6 to 8, cover 0.080 of it).

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = rng.exponential(scale=1/2, size=100_000)   # rate 2 per second, mean 0.5 s
print("share of waits <= 0.5 s:", np.mean(t <= 0.5))   # theory 1 - e^-1 = 0.632
print("share of waits > 1 s:  ", np.mean(t > 1))       # theory e^-2 = 0.135

print("P(Z <= 1.96)      =", round(norm.cdf(1.96), 4))
print("P(X > 85), N(70,10):", round(1 - norm.cdf(85, loc=70, scale=10), 4))
print("two tails beyond 2.02:", round(2 * (1 - norm.cdf(2.02)), 4))
blocks.caption: Output: share of waits <= 0.5 s 0.63301, share > 1 s 0.13535, P(Z <= 1.96) = 0.975, P(X > 85) = 0.0668, two tails beyond 2.02 = 0.0434. The simulated shares match 1 - e^-1 and e^-2 to about 3 decimals. NumPy's exponential takes scale = 1 / rate.

blocks.md: A density value is not a probability. A density of 2 does not mean probability 2, and the probability of any single exact value is 0, which is why $<$ and $\le$ give the same answer for continuous variables.
The CDF turns any range question into a subtraction, $F(b) - F(a)$. Standardizing turns any normal question into the standard normal CDF, $\Phi$.

blocks.question: X is uniform on [0, 0.5]. Which statement is true?
options: Its density cannot exceed 1, so it is 1 on the interval
P(X = 0.25) = 2, the density there
Its density is 2 on the interval, and P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.2
P(0.1 <= X <= 0.2) = 0.1, the length of the range
blocks.explain: The area must be 1 over a width of 0.5, so the height is 2. A range probability is width times height: 0.1 x 2 = 0.2. The length alone (0.1) is only right when the density is 1, and any single exact value has probability 0.

blocks.question: Response times are modeled (simplified) as normal with mean 50 ms and standard deviation 5 ms. About what fraction exceeds 60 ms?
options: About 16%
About 5%
About 0.3%
About 2.3%
blocks.explain: Standardize: z = (60 - 50) / 5 = 2, and 1 - Phi(2) = 0.023. 5% is the two-sided share beyond 1.96, and 16% is the share above 1 standard deviation. Real latencies are right-skewed, so a normal model understates the tail.

lessons.title: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT

blocks.md: Everything in statistics rests on one fact: the average of many independent samples is far more predictable than any single sample. Mini-batch gradients (training averages the gradient of the loss over a small random batch of examples), eval accuracies and A/B test conversion rates are all averages, so this lesson explains how much you can trust each of them. An **A/B test** shows two versions, A and B, to two random groups of users; a **conversion rate** is the fraction who click or buy.

blocks.title: Running average of 12 die rolls

scenes.caption: Twelve rolls of a fair die (generated with a seeded random number generator). The true mean is 3.5.
Early on, each new roll moves the average a lot: a 1 after four rolls pulls it from 3.75 to 3.2.
After 12 rolls the average is 3.08. A 13th roll would shift it by less than 0.25, because it would be 1 of 13. With thousands of rolls it would settle very close to 3.5.

blocks.md: The **law of large numbers** (LLN) says that the sample mean $\bar X_n = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ of independent, identically distributed (**i.i.d.**) samples converges to the true mean $\mu$ as $n$ grows. How fast? Use the rules from lesson 5: the variance of a sum of $n$ independent copies is $n\sigma^2$, and dividing by $n$ divides the variance by $n^2$.

blocks.caption: The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the sample mean. It shrinks with the square root of n.

blocks.prompt: Your eval accuracy has a standard error of 2 percentage points on 500 questions. How many questions do you need to cut that to 1 point?
blocks.reveal: **2,000 questions, not 1,000.** The standard error scales as $1/\sqrt n$, so halving it needs 4 times the data. Every extra digit of precision costs 100 times more samples.

blocks.md: The **central limit theorem** (CLT) says more: for i.i.d. samples with finite variance, the *shape* of the distribution of $\bar X_n$ approaches a normal curve with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt n$, whatever the shape of a single sample. Why a bell (intuition, not a proof): a sum of many independent pieces lands far from its mean only if most pieces are extreme in the same direction at once, which is rare, while there are many combinations that land near the middle. Finite variance rules out pieces so wild that one single value can dominate the whole sum (the Cauchy callout below shows what goes wrong). Watch it happen to a very non-normal variable: a click that happens with probability $p = 0.25$.

blocks.title: Distribution of the observed click rate in n impressions (p = 0.25)

scenes.caption: n = 1: the observed rate is 0 (probability 0.75) or 1 (probability 0.25). Two spikes, nothing like a bell. Exact binomial probabilities, grouped into bins that include their lower edge (a rate of 0.3 counts in 0.3-0.4).
n = 10: already a single hump around 0.25, though still lopsided. Only 28% of runs land in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin. Standard error 0.137.
n = 40: narrower and more symmetric, 53% of runs in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin. Standard error 0.068, half of the n = 10 value because n is 4 times larger.
n = 160: 86% of runs in the 0.2 to 0.3 bin, standard error 0.034. The LLN concentrates the rate around 0.25; the CLT gives the bell shape around it.

blocks.title: Normal approximation to the sample proportion

scenes.caption: n = 10, p = 0.25: SE = 0.137, so the normal curve puts 95% of observed rates within about 0.27 of p; the exact binomial puts 98% there. The approximation is rough at this n, and the curve even leaks below 0.
n = 40: the curve is twice as tall and half as wide.
n = 160: SE = 0.034. The band between the lines holds 95% of the mass: p plus or minus 1.96 SE (1.96, not 2, because exactly 95% of a normal lies within 1.96 standard deviations).
n = 400: SE = 0.022. Try moving p toward 0.5 to see the spread grow, since p(1 - p) is largest there.

blocks.md: The CLT needs independent samples and a finite variance. Correlated samples (consecutive tokens, users who appear many times) have a larger true standard error than $\sigma/\sqrt n$. **Heavy-tailed** data, where extreme values are far more common than under a normal, converges slowly. The **Cauchy** distribution (the ratio of two independent standard normal variables) has tails so heavy that its mean does not exist, and the average never settles at all.

Noise in an average shrinks as $1/\sqrt n$. That single scaling law explains why larger batches give smoother gradients, why small evals are noisy, and why A/B tests need large samples to detect small effects.

blocks.question: Batch size 64 gives a gradient-estimate standard deviation of s (per coordinate, i.i.d. examples). Approximately what does batch size 256 give?
options: s, since batch size does not affect noise
blocks.explain: The mini-batch gradient is an average of per-example gradients, so its standard deviation scales as 1/sqrt(batch). Four times the batch gives sqrt(4) = 2 times less noise, so s/2. The variance falls by 4.

blocks.question: Which statement does the central limit theorem actually support?
options: With enough data, the individual data points become normally distributed
The sample mean of many i.i.d. finite-variance samples is approximately normal
Any average is normal, even of strongly correlated samples
Large samples remove bias from a skewed sampling method
blocks.explain: The CLT is about the distribution of the average (or sum), not the raw data: individual clicks are still 0 or 1. It needs independence and finite variance, and it says nothing about bias: a biased sample averages tightly around the wrong value.

lessons.title: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian

blocks.md: Lesson 5 warned that variances add only for independent variables, with a correction term called covariance. This lesson measures how two variables move together. Tiny dataset: five users, with hours of use $x$ = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and a satisfaction score $y$ = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. Both means are easy: $\bar x = 3$, $\bar y = 4$.

The **covariance** is the mean product of the two deviations from their means, $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$. A point that is above average in both, or below in both, adds a positive product; a point above in one and below in the other adds a negative one. From a sample you divide the summed products by $n - 1$ rather than $n$, for the reason lesson 9 explains (`np.cov` does this by default).

blocks.title: Covariance by hand: deviations, then products

scenes.caption: Five (x, y) pairs. Mean of x is 3, mean of y is 4.
Subtract the means. The first user is below average in both (-2, -2); the last is above in both (2, 1).
Multiply each pair: 4, 0, 0, 0, 2. Both nonzero products are positive, so x and y rise together. Sum 6, divided by n - 1 = 4: covariance 1.5.

blocks.md: Covariance has units (hours times score points), so its size depends on the units: measure $x$ in minutes and it grows 60 times. The **correlation** divides out both standard deviations, leaving a unitless number between -1 and 1. Here the sample standard deviations are 1.581 and 1.225, so $\rho = 1.5 / (1.581 \times 1.225) = 0.775$, a strong positive linear relationship. ($\rho$ is the Greek letter rho.)

blocks.caption: Covariance is the mean product of deviations; correlation is covariance rescaled by both standard deviations. Correlation 1 or -1 means the points lie exactly on a line.

blocks.title: 2,000 points binned into a grid, at three correlations

scenes.caption: A scatter plot binned into cells (darker means more points; columns are labeled by their lower edge). Correlation 0.9: the points hug a rising diagonal. Sample correlation 0.90.
Correlation 0: a round cloud, high x says nothing about y. Sample correlation -0.03, noise around the true 0.
Correlation -0.6: a falling, fatter band. Sample correlation -0.61. The sign gives the direction and the size gives how tight the band is.

blocks.prompt: Let x be -2, -1, 0, 1 or 2, each equally likely, and y = x squared. What is the correlation of x and y?
blocks.reveal: **Zero.** $E[x] = 0$ and $\text{Cov}(x, y) = E[x \cdot x^2] - E[x]E[x^2] = E[x^3] = 0$, because the cubes cancel in pairs. Yet $y$ is completely determined by $x$. Correlation measures only *linear* association, and a U-shape has none. Independent variables always have zero covariance, but zero covariance does not imply independence.

blocks.md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

For a random vector $X = (X_1, \dots, X_n)$, such as the features of one example, the **covariance matrix** $\Sigma$ (capital sigma) holds every pairwise covariance: $\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$. Its diagonal holds the variances and it is symmetric. Example: $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1.2 \\ 1.2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ means standard deviations 2 and 1 and correlation $1.2 / (2 \times 1) = 0.6$. Independent features give a diagonal $\Sigma$. Any weighted sum $a^\top X = a_1 X_1 + \dots + a_n X_n$ (a dot product with a fixed vector $a$) has variance $a^\top \Sigma a = \sum_i \sum_j a_i a_j \Sigma_{ij}$; for two variables that is $a_1^2 \Sigma_{11} + 2 a_1 a_2 \Sigma_{12} + a_2^2 \Sigma_{22}$. With $a = (1, 1)$ it is $4 + 1 + 2 \times 1.2 = 7.4$, the $\text{Var}(X + Y)$ rule from lesson 5.

blocks.caption: Variance of a weighted sum, and the multivariate normal density. Its height falls off with a squared distance from the mean in units set by Sigma (Sigma inverse undoes Sigma; det Sigma, its determinant, keeps the total volume 1), so equal-height curves are ellipses.

blocks.title: Contours of a 2D Gaussian (unit variances) as correlation changes

scenes.caption: Correlation 0, independent coordinates: the contours are circles. The inner one encloses 39% of the probability, the outer one 86.5%.
Correlation 0.6, the Sigma example rescaled to unit variances: the circles stretch into ellipses along the rising diagonal.
Correlation 0.9: a narrow ellipse. Knowing x1 now pins down x2 well, as in the first grid above.
Correlation -0.6: the same stretch along the falling diagonal.

blocks.md: To sample from $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)$, draw independent standard normals $z$ and set $x = \mu + L z$, where $L L^\top = \Sigma$ ($L^\top$, the **transpose**, is $L$ mirrored across its diagonal; you can check the product through the two equations below). A convenient $L$ is the **Cholesky factor** (after the French mathematician Andre-Louis Cholesky), the unique lower-triangular matrix with positive diagonal that does this. For our $\Sigma$, $L = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0.6 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$, so $x_1 = \mu_1 + 2 z_1$ and $x_2 = \mu_2 + 0.6 z_1 + 0.8 z_2$. The shared $z_1$ creates the correlation: $\text{Cov}(x_1, x_2) = 2 \times 0.6 = 1.2$ and $\text{Var}(x_2) = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

mu = np.array([10.0, 5.0])
Sigma = np.array([[4.0, 1.2],
                  [1.2, 1.0]])
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)        # lower triangular, L @ L.T == Sigma
print(L)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
z = rng.standard_normal((100_000, 2))  # independent N(0, 1) pairs
x = mu + z @ L.T                       # each row is mu + L z
print(np.round(x.mean(axis=0), 2))
print(np.round(np.cov(x.T), 2))
blocks.caption: Output: L = [[2. 0.] [0.6 0.8]], sample mean [10. 5.], sample covariance [[4.02 1.2] [1.2 1.]]. 100,000 samples of mu + L z reproduce the target mean and covariance.

blocks.md: One matrix, Sigma, holds every pairwise covariance. Any weighted sum has variance a-transpose Sigma a, and a Gaussian with covariance Sigma is just mu + L z with independent standard normals z.

blocks.question: Two features have variances 9 and 4 and covariance 3. What is their correlation?
options: 3, the covariance itself
About 0.083, which is 3 / (9 x 4)
0.5, which is 3 / (3 x 2)
blocks.explain: Divide the covariance by both standard deviations, the square roots of the variances: 3 / (3 x 2) = 0.5. Dividing by the variances themselves is a common slip.

blocks.question: Two features in your data have correlation 0. What can you safely conclude?
options: They are independent, so a model gains nothing from using both
They have no linear association, but one may still depend strongly on the other
Their covariance matrix is the identity
One of them is constant
blocks.explain: Zero correlation rules out a linear trend only; y = x squared on symmetric x has correlation 0 and full dependence. The covariance matrix is diagonal, but not the identity unless both variances are 1.

lessons.title: Estimating parameters from data: maximum likelihood

blocks.md: So far the parameters were known: a fair die, a 25% click rate. Statistics runs the other way: you see data and want the parameter. An **estimator** is a rule that turns a sample into a guess, such as the sample mean for $\mu$. Two properties matter. **Bias** is how far its average guess is from the truth; **variance** is how much the guess jumps between samples. The sample mean is unbiased, with variance $\sigma^2/n$ from lesson 7.

**Maximum likelihood estimation** (MLE) is the general recipe. Write the probability of the observed data as a function of the parameter, called the **likelihood** $L(\theta)$ ($\theta$ is the usual name for an unknown parameter), and pick the $\theta$ that makes the data most probable. That pick is written $\hat\theta$: a hat marks an estimate. Example: a coin gives 7 heads in 10 i.i.d. flips. Under heads-probability $p$, that specific sequence has probability $p^7(1-p)^3$.

blocks.tex: L(p) = p^{7}(1-p)^{3}, \qquad \log L(p) = 7\log p + 3\log(1-p), \qquad \frac{d}{dp}\log L = \frac{7}{p} - \frac{3}{1-p} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \hat p = 0.7
blocks.caption: In words: take the log, 7 log p + 3 log(1 - p). Set its slope, 7/p - 3/(1 - p), to zero: 7(1 - p) = 3p, so p hat = 0.7, the observed share of heads. Taking the log turns the product over samples into a sum and does not move the maximum.

blocks.title: Likelihood of p, scaled so the peak is 1

scenes.caption: 7 heads in 10 flips: the peak is at 0.7. A fair coin (p = 0.5) still has 44% of the peak likelihood, so the data barely rule it out.
70 heads in 100 flips: same peak at 0.7, but now p = 0.5 has only 0.03% of the peak likelihood and p = 0.6 has 11.5%. More data sharpens the likelihood.
200 flips: sharper still. The width shrinks roughly as 1 over sqrt(n), the same scaling as the standard error.

blocks.md:
This is where most ML loss functions come from. A classifier sees input $x_i$ with label $y_i$ (0 or 1) and outputs $\hat y_i = P(y_i = 1 \mid x_i)$. The probability it gave to the true label is $\hat y_i$ if $y_i = 1$ and $1 - \hat y_i$ if $y_i = 0$, so the log of that is $y_i \log \hat y_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat y_i)$. Minus its average is the negative log-likelihood of the labels, the **binary cross-entropy** (a name from information theory, where minus the sum of $p \log q$ over outcomes, with $p$ the true distribution and $q$ the predicted one, is called the cross-entropy of $q$ relative to $p$; here $p$ puts all its weight on the true label). Minimizing cross-entropy *is* maximum likelihood; lesson 10 builds the term from entropy.

With softmax outputs (each class score $z_j$ becomes $e^{z_j} / \sum_k e^{z_k}$, a probability for each of several classes, summing to 1) it generalizes to categorical cross-entropy. A Gaussian likelihood with fixed variance gives mean squared error: the log of the normal density is $-(y - \hat y)^2 / (2\sigma^2)$ plus a constant.

blocks.caption: Average negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels (natural log): binary cross-entropy. For the 7-of-10 coin with p = 0.7 it is 0.611; with p = 0.5 it is log 2 = 0.693.

blocks.md: Maximum likelihood estimates are not always unbiased. The MLE of a normal variance divides the sum of squared deviations by $n$, which underestimates on average because the deviations are measured from the sample mean, which sits closer to the data than the true mean does. Exactly how much: $\sum (x_i - \mu)^2 = \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 + n(\bar x - \mu)^2$. The left side averages $n\sigma^2$ and the last term averages $n \times \sigma^2/n = \sigma^2$, so the sum around the sample mean averages $(n-1)\sigma^2$. Dividing by $n - 1$ (**Bessel's correction**, after the astronomer Friedrich Bessel) removes that bias.

blocks.title: Sample mean and the two variance estimators
blocks.code:
data = [2.0, 4.0, 4.0, 5.0, 7.0]
n = len(data)
mean = sum(data) / n
ss = 0.0
for x in data:
    ss += (x - mean) ** 2
var_mle = ss / n
var_unbiased = ss / (n - 1)
print(round(mean, 2), round(var_mle, 2), round(var_unbiased, 2))

scenes.caption: Five measurements. The sample mean is 22 / 5 = 4.4.
Sum the squared deviations from the sample mean: 5.76 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.36 + 6.76 = 13.2.
Divide by n for the MLE (2.64) or by n - 1 for the unbiased estimate (3.3). With 5 points the gap is 25%; it vanishes as n grows.

blocks.md: So which variance estimator is better? Judge an estimator by its **mean squared error**, $\text{MSE} = E[(\hat\theta - \theta)^2]$, the average squared miss, which splits into squared bias plus variance. For normal data with $n = 5$ and true $\sigma^2 = 1$, the $n - 1$ version is unbiased with variance $2/(n-1) = 0.5$, so its MSE is 0.5. The divide-by-$n$ version averages 0.8 (bias $-0.2$) but its variance is only 0.32, so its MSE is $0.04 + 0.32 = 0.36$, lower. Unbiased is not automatically best: accepting a little bias for a lot less variance is the bias-variance tradeoff, which returns whenever a model is fit to data.

blocks.caption: In words: the average squared miss equals how far the estimator is off on average, squared, plus how much it scatters around its own average.

blocks.title: Two variance estimators: bias squared, variance, MSE

scenes.caption: n = 5 normal samples, true variance 1 (theory, confirmed by 400,000 simulated datasets). The biased estimator wins on MSE: 0.36 vs 0.50.
n = 20: both MSEs shrink (0.0975 vs 0.105) and the bias of the n version falls to 0.05. Both estimators are consistent.

blocks.md: As $n$ grows, what you want most is that the estimate closes in on the truth: an estimator is **consistent** if, for any tolerance, the chance of missing by more than that tolerance goes to 0 as $n$ grows. Both variance estimators are consistent, because their bias and variance both shrink to 0. Unbiased does not imply consistent: using only the first data point as the estimate of the mean is unbiased for every $n$ but never improves.

In NumPy, `np.var(x)` divides by $n$ by default (`ddof=0`; ddof is "delta degrees of freedom" and the divisor is $n$ minus ddof), while `np.var(x, ddof=1)` divides by $n-1$. pandas `Series.var()` defaults to $n-1$. Check which one a library uses before comparing numbers.

A maximum likelihood estimate from little data can be extreme: 3 heads in 3 flips gives $\hat p = 1$, claiming tails is impossible. Priors (Bayes' rule again, lesson 11), smoothing such as adding pseudo-counts (pretend you saw one extra head and one extra tail: $\hat p = 4/5 = 0.8$), and regularization (a penalty in the loss that pulls parameters toward small values) all pull estimates away from such overconfident values.

blocks.question: A language model assigns probability 0.5 to every correct next token in a validation set. What is its average cross-entropy (natural log), and what does minimizing it on training data correspond to?
options: 0.5; minimizing the error rate
About 0.693; maximizing the likelihood of the training tokens
About 0.693; minimizing the variance of the predictions
1.0; maximizing accuracy
blocks.explain: Cross-entropy averages -log of the probability given to the correct token: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. Minimizing average negative log-likelihood over the training data is exactly maximum likelihood estimation of the model's parameters.

blocks.question: You compute the variance of 4 validation losses with np.var and compare it to a colleague's number computed with pandas on the same 4 values. Theirs is larger. Why?
options: pandas divides by n - 1 = 3, NumPy by n = 4, so theirs is 4/3 as large
pandas uses the population mean instead of the sample mean
NumPy squares the standard deviation twice
One of you has a bug, since variance is uniquely defined
blocks.explain: np.var defaults to ddof=0 (divide by n) and pandas Series.var defaults to ddof=1 (divide by n - 1). With 4 values the ratio is 4/3. Neither uses a population mean; both subtract the sample mean.

blocks.md: Lesson 9 called the classification loss *cross-entropy*. The name comes from **information theory**, which Claude Shannon founded in 1948 to study sending messages over noisy channels. Its starting intuition: learning that an unlikely event happened is more informative than learning that a likely one did. "The sun rose this morning" tells you almost nothing; "there was a solar eclipse this morning" tells you a lot.

The **self-information** (or surprise) of an outcome with probability $p$ is $-\log p$. A certain event has surprise 0, rarer events have more, and the surprises of independent events add, because the log of a product is a sum of logs. With the natural log the unit is the **nat**; with log base 2 it is the **bit**, and 1 nat is $1/\ln 2 = 1.443$ bits. A fair coin flip carries $-\ln 0.5 = 0.693$ nats, which is exactly 1 bit; an outcome with probability 0.1 carries 2.303 nats.

blocks.tex: I(x) = -\log P(x), \qquad H(P) = E_{x \sim P}\big[-\log P(x)\big] = -\sum_x P(x)\log P(x)
blocks.caption: Self-information of one outcome, and entropy: the average surprise when outcomes are drawn from P. The x ~ P under the E means x is drawn from P. By convention 0 log 0 counts as 0.

blocks.md: The **entropy** $H(P)$ is the expected surprise: how uncertain the distribution is. A fair coin has $\ln 2 = 0.693$ nats (1 bit). A coin with $P(\text{heads}) = 0.9$ has $-(0.9 \ln 0.9 + 0.1 \ln 0.1) = 0.325$ nats (0.469 bits). A certain outcome has 0. Measured in bits, entropy is a lower bound on the average number of bits any code needs per symbol drawn from $P$.

blocks.title: Entropy of a coin with P(heads) = p

scenes.caption: Entropy in nats peaks at p = 0.5 (0.693) and falls to 0 as the coin becomes certain either way.
The same curve in bits is just rescaled by 1 / ln 2: the fair coin is exactly 1 bit. Bits and nats are units, like miles and kilometers.

blocks.md: Now suppose outcomes come from $p$ but you score them with a model's probabilities $q$. The average surprise you experience is the **cross-entropy** $H(p, q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)$: in coding terms, the cost of encoding $p$'s outcomes with a code built for $q$. Three-class example with true distribution $p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)$: a close model $q_1 = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)$ and a bad one $q_2 = (0.1, 0.3, 0.6)$. $H(p) = 0.802$, $H(p, q_1) = 0.829$, $H(p, q_2) = 1.904$ nats.

blocks.title: True distribution p and two models

scenes.caption: The true distribution p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1). Its entropy, the best achievable average surprise, is 0.802 nats.
Model q1 = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) is close: cross-entropy 0.829 nats, only 0.027 above the entropy.
Model q2 = (0.1, 0.3, 0.6) puts little probability on the common class: cross-entropy 1.904 nats, 1.102 above the entropy.

blocks.tex: D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = H(p, q) - H(p) \;\ge\; 0
blocks.caption: KL divergence: the extra average surprise from using q instead of the true p. It is never negative and is 0 only when q equals p.

blocks.md: That gap is the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**, named after Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler, who defined it in 1951: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q_1) = 0.027$ and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q_2) = 1.102$ nats. It is often treated as a distance between distributions, but it is not symmetric: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_2 \| p) = 1.002$, not 1.102. Which direction you minimize changes what a model learns, so papers always state it.

Here is the payoff. In training, $p$ is the empirical distribution of the data and $q$ is the model. $H(p)$ depends only on the data, so minimizing the cross-entropy $H(p, q)$ over the model is the same as minimizing $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \| q)$, and lesson 9 showed it is also the same as maximizing likelihood. Any negative log-likelihood loss is a cross-entropy in this sense; mean squared error is the cross-entropy with a Gaussian model. With one-hot labels (all probability on the true class), $H(p) = 0$ and each example's loss is just $-\log q(\text{true class})$.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def H(p):      return -np.sum(p * np.log(p))
def CE(p, q):  return -np.sum(p * np.log(q))
def KL(p, q):  return np.sum(p * np.log(p / q))

p  = np.array([0.7, 0.2, 0.1])   # true label distribution
q1 = np.array([0.6, 0.3, 0.1])   # close model
q2 = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.6])   # bad model
print("H(p)      ", round(H(p), 3))
print("CE(p, q1) ", round(CE(p, q1), 3), " KL", round(KL(p, q1), 3))
print("CE(p, q2) ", round(CE(p, q2), 3), " KL", round(KL(p, q2), 3))
print("KL(q2, p) ", round(KL(q2, p), 3))
blocks.caption: Output: H(p) 0.802, CE(p, q1) 0.829 with KL 0.027, CE(p, q2) 1.904 with KL 1.102, KL(q2, p) 1.002. Natural log throughout, so the units are nats.

blocks.md: Language models report **perplexity**: $e$ raised to the average cross-entropy per token (or 2 raised to it, in bits). It reads as an effective number of choices. The model in lesson 9's quiz put 0.5 on every correct token: cross-entropy 0.693 nats, perplexity $e^{0.693} = 2$, as uncertain as a fair choice between 2 tokens at every step. Lower is better.

blocks.prompt: A classifier puts probability 0.001 on the true class of one example. How much does that example add to the cross-entropy, compared with a 50/50 guess?
blocks.reveal: $-\ln 0.001 = 6.91$ nats, about 10 times the 0.693 of a 50/50 guess. A probability of exactly 0 would cost infinitely much. Cross-entropy punishes confident mistakes far more than hesitant ones, so a few confidently wrong examples can dominate the average loss.

blocks.md: Check the log base before comparing numbers. Machine learning code and the Deep Learning book use the natural log (nats); information theory texts often use bits. Divide nats by $\ln 2 = 0.693$ to get bits.

Entropy is average surprise under the truth, cross-entropy is average surprise under your model, and KL divergence is the gap. Training on cross-entropy minimizes KL from the data, which is maximum likelihood.

blocks.question: Which statement about the KL divergence D(p || q) is true?
options: It is a true distance, so D(p || q) = D(q || p)
It can be negative when q is a better model than p
It equals the cross-entropy H(p, q) when the data are noisy
It is 0 only when q equals p, and swapping p and q can change it
blocks.explain: KL is never negative and is 0 only when the distributions match. It is not symmetric: for the example, 1.102 one way and 1.002 the other. It equals H(p, q) minus H(p), so it matches the cross-entropy only when H(p) = 0, as with one-hot labels.

blocks.question: A language model's average cross-entropy on a test set is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
options: About 7.4
About 0.14
blocks.explain: Perplexity is e to the cross-entropy in nats: e^2 = 7.39, as uncertain as choosing among about 7.4 equally likely tokens at each step. 4.0 would be 2 raised to 2.0, which is right only if the 2.0 were measured in bits.

lessons.title: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP

blocks.md: Lesson 9 ended with 3 heads in 3 flips: the maximum likelihood estimate is $\hat p = 1$, which claims tails is impossible. Bayes' rule from lesson 3 offers a fix. Treat the unknown heads probability $p$ itself as uncertain, with a **prior** distribution that says what you believe before the flips, and update it with the data to a **posterior**.

The convenient prior for a probability is the **beta distribution** Beta($a$, $b$) on $[0, 1]$, with density proportional to $p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}$. Beta(1, 1) is flat, every $p$ equally plausible. Multiply by the likelihood of $h$ heads and $t$ tails, $p^h(1-p)^t$, and the exponents just add: the posterior is Beta($a + h$, $b + t$). A prior that gives a posterior from the same family is called **conjugate**. So $a$ and $b$ act like counts: Beta(2, 2) is the flat prior plus one imagined head and one imagined tail.

blocks.caption: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior (lesson 3). The proportional sign hides the constant that makes the area 1, which is fixed by the shape.

blocks.md: A posterior is a whole distribution; two common one-number summaries are its peak, the **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate $(a-1)/(a+b-2)$, and its mean $a/(a+b)$. Prior Beta(2, 2) plus 3 heads in 3 flips gives Beta(5, 2): MAP $= 4/5 = 0.8$, exactly the pseudo-count estimate from lesson 9; posterior mean $5/7 = 0.714$; MLE 1.0.

blocks.title: Prior, likelihood and posterior for a coin (each scaled to peak 1)

scenes.caption: 3 heads, 0 tails. The likelihood climbs all the way to p = 1 (MLE 1.0); the prior pulls the posterior's peak back to 0.8.
7 heads, 3 tails: MLE 0.7, MAP 8/12 = 0.667. The prior still nudges the estimate toward 0.5.
21 heads, 9 tails: MLE 0.7, MAP 22/32 = 0.688. The likelihood now dominates and the posterior nearly coincides with it: the prior matters less as data grow.

blocks.md: MAP connects straight to regularization. Taking logs of posterior proportional to likelihood times prior, the MAP estimate maximizes the log-likelihood **plus a log-prior term**. Put a zero-mean Gaussian prior on a model's weights and the log-prior is a constant minus a multiple of $\sum_i w_i^2$: that is the L2 penalty, also called **weight decay**. A Laplace prior (after Pierre-Simon Laplace; a sharp peak at 0 with exponential tails) gives a multiple of $\sum_i |w_i|$, the L1 penalty. Regularized models in ML use both.

blocks.tex: \theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta \big[\log p(x \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta)\big], \qquad w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tfrac{1}{\lambda} I) \;\Rightarrow\; \log p(w) = -\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\, w^\top w + \text{const}
blocks.caption: In words: MAP is maximum likelihood with an extra term, the log of the prior. For a Gaussian prior with variance 1 / lambda on each weight, that term is minus lambda / 2 times the sum of squared weights. Arg max means the value of theta that maximizes the bracket.

blocks.title: Three estimates of the heads probability

scenes.caption: 3 heads in 3 flips: 1.000, 0.800, 0.714. With little data the prior moves the estimate a lot.
21 heads in 30 flips: 0.700, 0.688, 0.676. With ten times the data, the three nearly agree.

blocks.md: The posterior also gives intervals with a direct meaning. A 95% **credible interval** contains 95% of the posterior probability: for Beta(5, 2) the central one runs from 0.359 to 0.957, and you may say "given the prior and data, $p$ is in there with probability 0.95". A 95% **confidence interval** (lesson 12) makes a different promise: the *procedure* captures the fixed true value in 95% of repeated experiments, with no probability statement about one particular interval.

blocks.code:
from scipy.stats import beta

a0, b0 = 2, 2                  # prior Beta(2, 2): like 1 extra head, 1 extra tail
for heads, tails in [(3, 0), (21, 9)]:
    a, b = a0 + heads, b0 + tails
    mle  = heads / (heads + tails)
    map_ = (a - 1) / (a + b - 2)
    mean = a / (a + b)
    lo, hi = beta.ppf([0.025, 0.975], a, b)
    print(f"{heads}/{heads+tails}: MLE {mle:.3f} MAP {map_:.3f} "
          f"mean {mean:.3f} 95% credible [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")
blocks.caption: Output: 3/3: MLE 1.000 MAP 0.800 mean 0.714 95% credible [0.359, 0.957]; 21/30: MLE 0.700 MAP 0.688 mean 0.676 95% credible [0.513, 0.820]. The interval shrinks as data arrive.

blocks.prompt: Same 3 heads in 3 flips, but with the flat prior Beta(1, 1). What is the MAP estimate?
blocks.reveal: **1.0, the same as the MLE.** The posterior is Beta(4, 1), whose peak is $(4-1)/(4+1-2) = 1$. With a flat prior the log-prior is a constant, so maximizing the posterior is maximizing the likelihood. The posterior mean, $4/5 = 0.8$, still hedges, which is one reason to look at more than the peak.

blocks.md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.
Prior plus data gives a posterior. MAP is maximum likelihood plus a log-prior term, which is why L2 and L1 penalties are Gaussian and Laplace priors in disguise.

blocks.question: Prior Beta(3, 3). You observe 2 heads and 6 tails. What are the posterior and its MAP estimate?
options: Beta(5, 9), MAP 1/3
Beta(2, 6), MAP 0.25
Beta(5, 9), MAP 0.25, the same as the MLE
Beta(3, 3), since one small sample does not change the prior
blocks.explain: Add heads to a and tails to b: Beta(3 + 2, 3 + 6) = Beta(5, 9). MAP = (5 - 1) / (5 + 9 - 2) = 4/12 = 1/3, pulled from the MLE of 0.25 toward the prior's 0.5.

blocks.question: From the Bayesian point of view, training with an L2 penalty (weight decay) on the weights is:
options: Maximum likelihood with no prior
Computing the full posterior distribution over the weights
MAP estimation with a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights
MAP estimation with a flat prior
blocks.explain: The Gaussian log-prior is a constant minus a multiple of the sum of squared weights, which is the L2 penalty. A flat prior adds nothing, so its MAP equals the MLE. MAP gives one point, not the full posterior.

lessons.title: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test

blocks.md: A product team tests a new ranking model. Variant A (old) gets 200 clicks from 2,000 users, a 10.0% rate. Variant B (new) gets 240 clicks from 2,000 users, 12.0%. Is B really better, or could a 2 point gap appear by chance? The previous lessons give everything needed to answer.

A **95% confidence interval** is a range built by a procedure that, over many repeated experiments, captures the true value 95% of the time. By the CLT (lesson 7), an estimate $\hat\theta$ is roughly normal around the true value, with spread equal to its standard error (SE), and 95% of a normal lies within 1.96 standard deviations, so the interval is $\hat\theta \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$. For A alone, the Bernoulli variance $p(1-p)$ divided by $n$ gives $\text{SE} = \sqrt{0.1 \times 0.9 / 2000} = 0.0067$, giving 8.7% to 11.3%.

blocks.tex: \text{SE}(\hat p_B - \hat p_A) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p_A(1-\hat p_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat p_B(1-\hat p_B)}{n_B}} = 0.0099, \qquad 0.020 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0099 = [0.0006,\ 0.0394]
blocks.caption: In words: square each arm's SE (0.000045 for A, 0.0000528 for B), add them because variances of independent estimates add, and take the square root: 0.0099. The interval 0.020 plus or minus 1.96 times 0.0099 runs from 0.0006 to 0.0394, that is 0.06 to 3.94 points, and barely excludes 0.

blocks.md: A **hypothesis test** asks the same question differently. Assume the **null hypothesis** $H_0$: both variants share one true rate. Under $H_0$ there is only one rate, so its best estimate pools all users: $\hat p = 440/4000 = 0.11$ and a standard error under $H_0$ of $\sqrt{0.11 \times 0.89 \times (1/2000 + 1/2000)} = 0.0099$. The **z statistic** is the observed difference in standard errors: $z = 0.02 / 0.0099 = 2.02$. Under $H_0$ this ratio follows the standard normal distribution of lesson 6, which is why it is called z. The **p-value** is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ and the model are true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; a gap in either direction counts (two-sided), so it is the area of both tails beyond $\pm z$.

blocks.title: Where the observed z falls under the null hypothesis

scenes.caption: If there were no real difference, z would follow this curve. Only 5% of the area lies beyond plus or minus 1.96.
Observed z = 2.02, just past 1.96. The two-sided p-value, the area beyond plus or minus 2.02, is 0.043.
Same 10% vs 12% rates with 8,000 users per arm: z = 4.04, p = 0.00005. The effect did not change, only the sample size; the 95% interval narrows to 1.0 to 3.0 points.

blocks.md: Here $p = 2\,(1 - \Phi(2.02)) = 0.043$, using the standard normal CDF $\Phi$ from lesson 6. It is below the common threshold $\alpha = 0.05$, so the result is called statistically significant. $\alpha$ is the false positive rate you accept: when $H_0$ is true, a 0.05 threshold rejects it 5% of the time.

The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement lists the usual misreadings. A p-value is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true (that is the Bayes' rule mix-up from lesson 3), it does **not** measure the size or importance of an effect, and decisions should not rest only on whether it crosses 0.05. Report the effect size (here the 2 point gap) and its confidence interval.

blocks.prompt: You test 20 different model tweaks, none of which actually helps, each at alpha = 0.05 with independent data. How likely is it that at least one looks significant?
blocks.reveal: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$. **Better than even odds of a false discovery.** Testing many variants, metrics or user segments, or checking a running test repeatedly and stopping at the first significant peek (lesson 13 simulates it), inflates false positives the same way. Corrections such as Bonferroni (use $\alpha / k$ for $k$ tests: the chance of any false positive is at most the sum of the $k$ chances, $k \times \alpha/k = \alpha$) or pre-registering one primary metric (writing it down before seeing any data) control this.

blocks.title: Chance of at least one false positive across k null tests

scenes.caption: One test at alpha = 0.05: a 5% false positive rate, as designed.
Independent tests compound: 1 - 0.95^k gives 22.6% for 5 tests, 40.1% for 10, 64.2% for 20 and 92.3% for 50.

blocks.md: The $\pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$ interval for a proportion (the Wald interval, which computes SE from the observed rate) behaves poorly with small counts or rates near 0 or 1. The NIST handbook uses the Wilson interval instead (from Edwin Wilson, 1927), noting it was recommended for virtually all combinations of n and p: it keeps every rate $p$ whose own SE, $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, puts the observed rate within 1.96 SE, so it stays inside 0 to 1.

Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

blocks.question: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for a lift in click rate. Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 3% chance the new variant is not better
There is a 97% chance the lift is real
If there were no true difference, a gap this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time
The lift is large enough to matter for the business
blocks.explain: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true: it is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0 | data). Getting the probability that the variant is better needs a prior and Bayes' rule. And p says nothing about whether the effect size matters.

blocks.question: Two experiments find the same 0.2 point lift in conversion. Experiment 1 (50,000 users) has p = 0.01; experiment 2 (5,000 users) has p = 0.40. What is the best conclusion?
options: Experiment 2 shows the lift is absent
The experiments contradict each other
Both are consistent with the same lift; experiment 2 is too small to distinguish it from noise
Experiment 1 must have a bug, since the lifts match but p differs
blocks.explain: Same effect, ten times fewer users means a standard error about sqrt(10) = 3.2 times larger, so a much smaller z and larger p. A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; its confidence interval is just wide enough to include 0.

lessons.title: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it

blocks.md: Lesson 12 read a finished test. The decision that matters comes earlier: how many users should it have? A test can be wrong in two ways. A **Type I error** rejects $H_0$ when it is true, a false positive, with probability $\alpha$. A **Type II error** fails to reject $H_0$ when there is a real effect, a false negative, with probability $\beta$. The **power** is $1 - \beta$: the probability the test detects an effect of a given size when it is really there.

blocks.title: Decision probabilities for the 10% vs 12% test

scenes.caption: Top row, no real effect: the test wrongly rejects 5% of the time (alpha, Type I). Bottom row, a real 2 point lift with 2,000 users per arm: it detects it only 52.5% of the time (power) and misses it 47.5% of the time (Type II).
Same effect with 3,839 users per arm: power rises to 80% and misses fall to 20%. The false positive rate stays at 5%, set by alpha alone.
